name: webappanalyzer
maintainer: Enthec (community continuation of Wappalyzer's open-source line)
purpose: Maintained ruleset identifying the technologies behind a website — frameworks, analytics, CDNs, CRM and marketing platforms — continuing the open fingerprint database after Wappalyzer's open-source version was discontinued.
journalism_use_case: Establishing which commercial services a government or company website runs on, which is how you show that a state agency processes citizen data through a foreign CRM or that a propaganda network shares a single obscure analytics platform — the technology stack is both a privacy story and a network-attribution signal.
pros: Technology fingerprinting serves two distinct investigative purposes at once: documenting third-party data processing, and linking apparently unrelated sites that share unusual infrastructure
Community continuation of a discontinued commercial open-source project, so the fingerprint database remains usable without a vendor subscription — a genuine rescue
Plain ruleset data rather than a service, so you can apply it in your own pipeline and keep the analysis private
Maintained with current updates and an identifiable steward (Enthec)
cons: It is a ruleset, not a tool: you need a detection engine to apply it, so there is integration work before you get results
Fingerprint rules produce false positives and miss in-house or unusual technologies, so attribution of a shared platform should be verified by another signal before publication
Community continuations carry continuity risk — the original line was discontinued once, and this is a smaller effort than the commercial product
Technology detection from the client side sees only what the page exposes, so server-side processing arrangements remain invisible
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. The relevant documented context is the lineage: Wappalyzer's open-source version was discontinued and this is the community continuation, which session 1 recorded in its FORKS map and which this session retained. Maintenance was verified from the repository metadata.
assessment: Integrate it as the fingerprint database behind whatever detection you run, and treat its output as a lead. For your profile the more interesting use is the second one: shared unusual infrastructure across several sites is a strong hypothesis of common operation, which is how disinformation-network attribution often starts — but confirm with registration data, certificate overlap or analytics identifiers before publishing a link.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as a live, non-archived repository receiving updates, maintained by Enthec as the community continuation of Wappalyzer's discontinued open-source fingerprint database. Maintenance here means ruleset updates rather than software releases, so cadence is assessed on commit activity.
licence: MIT (community continuation licensing — verify the repository licence file for your records)
model_or_data_licence: The fingerprint ruleset is the deliverable; check its terms before redistributing it as a dataset.
licence_restrictions: Permissive as published; confirm from the repository before embedding the ruleset in a distributed product, since the lineage from a formerly commercial project warrants a check.
costs: No fee. Negligible — it is a data repository. Cost is building or adopting a detection engine.
privacy: Applying the ruleset locally keeps your analysis private; the detection requests themselves are visible to the target sites.
alternatives: WhatWeb for a self-contained fingerprinting CLI
SiteOne Crawler for a report-oriented technology inventory
AnalyticsRelationships specifically for linking sites via shared analytics identifiers
summary: Maintained ruleset identifying the technologies behind a website — frameworks, analytics, CDNs, CRM and marketing platforms…

name: WhatWeb
purpose: Web technology fingerprinting scanner with over a thousand plugins that identifies content management systems, frameworks, analytics, server software and embedded devices, with configurable aggression levels.
journalism_use_case: Fingerprinting a target's web infrastructure in one command: identify the CMS and server stack of a surveillance vendor's site, or sweep a list of suspected front organisations to find which share an unusual platform. The device-detection plugins also identify exposed appliances, which matters when mapping surveillance infrastructure.
pros: Self-contained CLI with its own plugin database, so unlike webappanalyzer you get results immediately with no engine to build
Aggression levels let you choose between passive identification and active probing, which is both an accuracy and an operational-security control
Identifies embedded devices and appliances as well as web stacks, useful when the subject is physical surveillance infrastructure exposed to the internet
Long-established tool packaged in security distributions, so it is available and familiar
cons: Active scanning modes send probes that are detectable and may be logged as hostile by the target — an operational-security and potentially legal consideration when the target is a surveillance company
Ruby-based with a plugin architecture of considerable age; maintenance is steady rather than brisk and the plugin database ages against modern JavaScript-heavy sites
Fingerprints are inferences and produce false positives, so an attribution based on a single match is weak
Security-tooling heritage means the defaults and documentation assume penetration-testing context rather than journalism
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with a substantial history; maintenance is steady rather than frequent. WhatWeb's standing as a fingerprinting tool is established by its inclusion in standard security distributions.
assessment: Keep it for quick reconnaissance, with the aggression level set low when the target would object to being probed. For your profile the practical pairing is WhatWeb for a first pass and certificate-transparency plus registry data for attribution, because fingerprint matches alone will not survive a challenge. Treat scanning a surveillance vendor's infrastructure as a visible act and route it through an egress that is not your newsroom.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived. A mature Ruby tool with a long release history and steady rather than frequent updates; the plugin database is the component that matters and it ages gradually against modern sites.
licence: GPL-2.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file for your records)
licence_restrictions: GPL-family copyleft on the tool; immaterial for internal use. Active scanning may engage computer-misuse law depending on jurisdiction and target — a legal rather than licence question.
costs: No fee. Ruby runtime; negligible resources.
privacy: Scanning is visible to the target. Passive modes reduce but do not eliminate the footprint; use a dedicated egress for sensitive targets.
alternatives: webappanalyzer ruleset applied in your own pipeline for a quieter approach
httpx for fast HTTP probing across many hosts
Passive sources (certificate transparency, DNS history) which leave no trace with the target
blockers: Active scanning is detectable and may engage computer-misuse law
summary: Web technology fingerprinting scanner with over a thousand plugins that identifies content management systems, frameworks…

name: AnalyticsRelationships
purpose: Tool that extracts analytics identifiers (Google Analytics, Tag Manager and similar) from a website and searches for other domains using the same identifier, revealing sites under common management.
journalism_use_case: One of the most productive attribution techniques in disinformation and front-company investigation: a network of ostensibly unrelated news sites sharing a single Google Analytics property is strong evidence of common operation, and this automates finding that overlap.
pros: Shared analytics identifiers are among the strongest technical links between websites, because they imply shared administrative access rather than merely similar technology — materially better evidence than a shared CDN or framework
Automates a technique that is otherwise manual and tedious, which is what makes it usable across a list of suspected sites
Small, readable tool that can be adapted, with no infrastructure requirement
Directly serves the B2 purpose: mapping which entities operate which online properties
cons: Depends on third-party reverse-analytics search services whose coverage, availability and terms are outside your control — the capability can degrade without warning
Shared identifiers can also result from a shared web developer or agency rather than common ownership, so the finding needs corroboration before it becomes an attribution in print
Small project with a modest community, so maintenance and continuity are uncertain and you may end up owning it
Queries disclose the domains you are investigating to the reverse-analytics services used
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with a small community. The underlying technique is well established in published open-source investigations into website networks, which is the relevant evidence that it works.
assessment: Adopt the technique, and use this tool as the convenient implementation while remaining ready to do it by hand. For your profile the methodological discipline is what matters: a shared analytics ID is a hypothesis of common operation, and before publishing you want a second independent link (registration data, certificate overlap, shared hosting, content reuse) plus an explanation of why a shared agency is not the simpler explanation.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived, but with a small community and no substantial release cadence. Because the capability depends on third-party reverse-analytics services rather than on the code, repository activity is a weak indicator of whether the tool still works — classified Uncertain for that reason rather than inferring health from either direction.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Third-party reverse-analytics services have their own terms.
licence_restrictions: Permissive as published; the operative constraints are the third-party services' terms of use.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute. The third-party services it queries may have rate limits or paid tiers (not verified in this survey).
privacy: Queries disclose the domains under investigation to the reverse-analytics services. Use a dedicated egress for sensitive attribution work.
alternatives: Manual extraction of analytics identifiers plus a reverse-lookup service, which is the same technique without a dependency
Certificate-transparency overlap (certstream, crt.sh) for an attribution signal that leaves no trace with third parties
DNS and WHOIS history for registration-based attribution
blockers: Depends on third-party reverse-analytics services whose availability and terms are outside your control
summary: Tool that extracts analytics identifiers (Google Analytics, Tag Manager and similar) from a website and searches for other…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: certstream-server
purpose: Server that aggregates certificate-transparency logs into a real-time stream of newly issued TLS certificates, with a websocket API for consumers.
journalism_use_case: Watching a surveillance vendor's infrastructure appear in real time: new certificates reveal new subdomains and hostnames as they are provisioned, so you learn about a new command-and-control domain, a new product environment or a renamed service before it is announced — and entirely passively, with no contact with the target.
pros: Passive by construction: certificate-transparency logs are public and reading them involves no interaction with the target, which is the ideal operational-security profile for monitoring an adversary
Real-time notification of new infrastructure is a genuine early-warning capability — infrastructure appears in CT logs before it appears anywhere else
Self-hostable, so your monitoring interests are not disclosed to a service operator
Underpins much of the certificate-monitoring tooling in this field, so understanding it explains the category
cons: High-volume stream: certificate issuance across the web is enormous, so useful monitoring requires filtering logic and storage design rather than just connecting

Self-hosting means consuming and processing a very large data flow, which is real infrastructure; using a public CertStream instance discloses nothing directly but makes you dependent on its continuity
Certificates reveal hostnames, not ownership, so attribution still requires registry and WHOIS work
Maintenance cadence is modest and the project is small relative to its importance in the ecosystem
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived. Certificate-transparency monitoring is a well-established technique in both security research and open-source investigation, and CertStream is its best-known open implementation.
assessment: Integrate it if you monitor specific adversaries over time — for a surveillance-industry beat, a filtered CT feed on a vendor's known domains is one of the highest-value, lowest-risk monitoring capabilities you can build. For your profile the practical design is to consume a public stream (or self-host if volume and privacy justify it), filter on a watchlist of domain patterns, and alert into an internal channel. Pair with Metabigor or RIR lookups for the ownership question that certificates cannot answer.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived, with modest activity. The project is a mature piece of infrastructure in a niche where the underlying data source (CT logs) is externally guaranteed, so low code velocity carries less risk than it would elsewhere.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Certificate-transparency log data is public by design.
licence_restrictions: Permissive as published. CT log data carries no usage restriction of consequence.
costs: No fee. Self-hosting estimate: sustained bandwidth and processing for a high-volume stream plus storage for whatever you retain — a real but modest infrastructure commitment; filtering at ingest keeps it small. Assumptions: watchlist-filtered retention rather than full archival.
privacy: Entirely passive with respect to the target: reading CT logs involves no contact with the monitored infrastructure. Self-hosting also keeps your watchlist private, which a public-stream consumer with server-side filtering would not.
alternatives: crt.sh for interactive certificate searches without running infrastructure
Commercial CT monitoring services, which are easier and disclose your watchlist
dnstwist for detecting lookalike domains rather than monitoring known ones
summary: Server that aggregates certificate-transparency logs into a real-time stream of newly issued TLS certificates…

name: Mihari
purpose: Framework for continuous threat-hunting that runs saved queries against many data sources (scan databases, certificate logs, passive DNS, URL scanners), deduplicates results into alerts and tracks artefacts over time.
journalism_use_case: Turning one-off infrastructure discovery into a standing watch: define queries describing a surveillance vendor's infrastructure patterns and have Mihari alert you when new matching hosts appear across several data sources — the difference between finding a vendor's servers once and tracking how its estate changes over a year.
pros: Multi-source querying with deduplication is the right architecture for infrastructure monitoring, because no single scan database has adequate coverage and manually reconciling them is unsustainable
Artefact tracking over time builds a longitudinal picture, which is what supports a story about how an operation grew or moved
Self-hosted, so your queries and watchlists remain private — important when the watchlist is effectively a list of your investigative targets
Alerting model fits a beat rather than a project: it keeps working while you do other things
cons: Depends on API keys for the underlying scan databases (Shodan, Censys and similar), several of which are paid — so the real cost is the data subscriptions, not the tool

Your queries are sent to those commercial providers, which therefore learn your investigative targets — the same exposure as uncover, compounded by the fact that monitoring is continuous rather than one-off
Security-operations orientation means the concepts (artefacts, alerts, enrichers) take orientation for a journalist, and the documentation assumes that background
Small project relative to its ambition, so continuity depends on a single maintainer
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with an active development pattern. Mihari is known in the threat-intelligence community as a lightweight alternative to commercial hunting platforms, which is the relevant adjacent context.
assessment: Worth piloting if surveillance-industry infrastructure is a sustained beat rather than an occasional story — the longitudinal tracking is what produces findings competitors do not have. For your profile the decisive considerations are budget and disclosure: paid scan-database subscriptions are the real cost, and continuous querying tells those vendors exactly who you are watching, so use accounts and egress that are not attributable to your newsroom and consider whether passive sources (certificate transparency, passive DNS) can carry more of the load.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with ongoing development from a single maintainer. Classified stable-low because the project is small and maintenance depends on one person, while the capability depends on external data sources rather than on code velocity.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Data comes from the configured commercial and public sources under their own terms, several of which restrict redistribution.
licence_restrictions: Permissive as published. The binding constraints are the scan vendors' API terms, which typically prohibit redistributing their data — relevant if you want to publish a dataset of findings.
costs: Software free. Real cost is paid API subscriptions to scan databases (Shodan, Censys, FOFA and similar — prices not verified in this survey) plus a small VM. Budget the data, not the tool.
privacy: Self-hosting keeps the system private, but the queries themselves go to commercial providers who learn your continuous watchlist. This is the central trade-off and should drive your choice of data sources.
alternatives: certstream-server plus your own filtering for a fully passive, no-disclosure watch
uncover for one-off multi-database queries rather than continuous monitoring
Commercial threat-intelligence platforms, which are more capable, expensive and equally disclosing
blockers: Continuous querying discloses your investigative watchlist to commercial scan vendors; several required APIs are paid
summary: Framework for continuous threat-hunting that runs saved queries against many data sources (scan databases, certificate logs…

name: OpenOversight
purpose: Public, crowdsourced database and web application for identifying police officers from photographs and badge numbers, linking officers to departments, assignments and complaint records.
journalism_use_case: Identifying officers in protest footage or complaint records — the specific accountability problem where a journalist has an image and a badge number but no name, and where departments decline to assist. It is also a model for building an identifiable-public-official database in other jurisdictions.
pros: Addresses a concrete accountability gap that journalists hit repeatedly, and does so with a crowdsourcing model that scales beyond what one newsroom could compile
Self-hostable, so the approach is transferable to other jurisdictions and other categories of public official where records exist but are not searchable
Built by a civil-liberties organisation with an explicit accountability purpose, so the data model and ethics are oriented to public-interest use
Open source, so the methodology for assembling such a database is inspectable and reusable
cons: Jurisdiction-specific in practice: the deployed instances cover particular US departments, so outside those it is a template rather than a resource

Building and operating such a database raises serious legal and ethical questions — data protection, accuracy obligations, the consequences of a wrong identification — that are entirely on the operator and are heavier outside the US
A crowdsourced identification is a lead, not a fact: publishing a name from a photographic match without independent confirmation would be indefensible
Small project with a specialist focus, so maintenance capacity is limited and a self-hosted deployment means owning the code
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived. Lucy Parsons Labs operates public instances and the project's accountability purpose is documented, which is the relevant context; I verified no specific newsroom use.
assessment: Relevant mainly as a model unless you work in a covered US jurisdiction. For your profile the transferable idea is strong — a searchable database of identifiable public officials, built from public records, is a durable accountability asset — but the legal exposure differs sharply by jurisdiction, and in Europe a comparable database of named officials with photographs would need a serious data-protection assessment before a line of code was written. Treat identifications as leads requiring independent confirmation.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived, maintained by a small civil-liberties organisation at modest velocity. Operating instances exist, which is the stronger signal for a database project than commit frequency.
licence: GPL-3.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: The database contents are compiled from public records and crowdsourced contributions; terms vary by instance and jurisdiction.
licence_restrictions: Copyleft on the application. The substantive constraints are data-protection law and accuracy obligations, which differ by jurisdiction and are far more restrictive than the software licence.
costs: No software fee. Self-hosting is a web application plus image storage — modest. The real costs are legal review and the editorial labour of verifying records. Estimate.
privacy: The project's purpose is to make public officials identifiable, so its privacy posture is deliberately asymmetric: it protects contributors and exposes officials acting in a public capacity. Operating an instance makes you a data controller with the obligations that follow, which in some jurisdictions is a substantial undertaking.
alternatives: Direct public-records requests for officer rosters and assignments
A purpose-built internal database (Datasette over curated records) scoped to one investigation
Collaboration with a local civil-liberties organisation that already holds the records
blockers: Jurisdiction-specific coverage; operating a comparable database raises significant data-protection obligations outside the US
summary: Public, crowdsourced database and web application for identifying police officers from photographs and badge numbers…

name: TED — Tenders Electronic Daily (EU public procurement)
maintainer: Publications Office of the European Union
purpose: Official EU portal publishing public-procurement notices above threshold from all member states, including contract notices, award notices and contracting-authority details, with search and bulk data access.
journalism_use_case: The primary record for European surveillance procurement: finding which ministry or police force bought interception, forensic or biometric systems, from which supplier and for how much. Award notices name the winning bidder and value, which is the documentary core of a surveillance-procurement story.
pros: Official, authoritative and citable: a TED award notice is a primary document, which is far stronger than a vendor press release or a leaked slide
Covers all EU member states in one place, so cross-border comparison of what different governments bought is tractable
Bulk and API access exist alongside the web search, so systematic monitoring of procurement categories is possible rather than only ad-hoc lookups
Free to access with no account required for search
cons: Only above-threshold procurement is published, and surveillance purchases are frequently structured below threshold, through framework agreements, through intermediaries, or exempted on national-security grounds — so absence from TED is not absence of purchase, and this is the central analytical limitation
Notice text is terse and uses procurement vocabulary and CPV codes rather than product names, so identifying surveillance purchases requires knowing how they are described

Session 1's recorded URL (ted.europa.eu/en/simple-search) returns 404; the current entry point is ted.europa.eu/en/ (verified 2026-11-17) — the portal has been restructured, which also affects saved searches and scraping code
Not open-source software and not a dataset you control: access terms, structure and availability are the EU's to change, as the URL change demonstrates
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the session-1 URL now 404s while the portal root returns 200 (both verified 2026-11-17 and recorded in sources/evidence/b2-sources.md). TED's role in European procurement journalism is well established; the under-threshold and national-security exemptions are documented features of the EU procurement regime.
assessment: Adopt it as a primary source and build a standing search on the relevant CPV codes and keywords rather than searching reactively. For your profile the analytical discipline matters most: a TED notice proves a purchase, while the absence of notices proves nothing, because national-security exemptions and framework agreements hide exactly the procurement you care about. Pair TED with national procurement portals, parliamentary questions and export-licence records to triangulate. Fix any saved searches or scrapers against the restructured portal.
maintenance_evidence: Portal verified live on 2026-11-17 (ted.europa.eu/en/ returns 200). It is an operational EU statutory publication service rather than a software project, so maintenance is institutional; the restructuring that broke the older URL is itself evidence of ongoing development.
licence: EU reuse terms apply to TED data (generally permissive with attribution under the Commission's reuse decision) — specific current terms NOT verified in this survey
model_or_data_licence: Same. Verify the current reuse notice before republishing bulk data.
licence_restrictions: Not verified here. EU public-sector information is generally reusable with attribution, but confirm the current terms before publishing a derived dataset.
costs: Free to search and access. Infrastructure cost only if you build a monitoring pipeline over the bulk data. No fee verified.
privacy: Searching the portal discloses your queries to the EU service in the ordinary way. The records concern public bodies and their suppliers, not individuals.
alternatives: National procurement portals for below-threshold and nationally exempted contracts
data.europa.eu for related EU open datasets
Open Contracting Data Standard-formatted national publications where available
blockers: Above-threshold publication only; national-security exemptions hide much surveillance procurement
summary: Official EU portal publishing public-procurement notices above threshold from all member states, including contract notices…
oss_detail: Hosted service or proprietary software — governed by service terms, not a software licence

name: USAspending.gov (custom award data)
maintainer: US Department of the Treasury / Bureau of the Fiscal Service
purpose: Official US federal spending portal with searchable and bulk-downloadable award data covering contracts, grants and subawards, including recipient, agency, amount, date and product/service codes.
journalism_use_case: Establishing which US federal agencies bought surveillance and forensic technology, from whom and for how much — including the Cellebrite, Magnet Forensics and biometric-system contracts that recur in surveillance reporting. The custom download lets you extract an entire category of spending for analysis rather than clicking through records.
pros: Authoritative primary data with recipient names, amounts and dates, downloadable in bulk — the strongest openly available procurement dataset of any jurisdiction
Product and service codes (PSC) and NAICS classification let you isolate a technology category systematically rather than keyword-guessing
Subaward data is included, which is how you find the integrator-to-vendor relationships that keep a surveillance supplier's name off the prime contract
US federal government works are generally public domain, so republication and derived datasets are straightforward
cons: Classified and some national-security procurement is excluded or redacted, so the most sensitive surveillance purchases may simply be absent — the same structural limitation as TED
Data quality is uneven: recipient naming is inconsistent, requiring entity resolution (rigour plus Splink) before aggregate figures are trustworthy
Large bulk downloads are unwieldy, and the custom-download interface imposes limits that shape how you have to query
US only, so it is irrelevant for non-US procurement questions except where a US supplier or subsidiary is involved
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the download-centre URL was verified live on 2026-11-17 (200). USAspending is widely used in US accountability journalism, and the inconsistent-recipient-naming problem is a well-known characteristic of the dataset rather than a criticism of the portal.
assessment: Adopt it as the primary source for US surveillance procurement and plan for entity resolution as a first-class step — the names are messy enough that aggregate totals are wrong without it. For your profile the high-value technique is combining prime and subaward data: a vendor absent from prime contracts often appears as a subcontractor, and that linkage is where the story usually is. Note that absence of a contract is not evidence of no purchase, given classified procurement.
maintenance_evidence: Portal and download centre verified live on 2026-11-17 (200). A statutory US government service with continuous publication; maintenance is institutional rather than release-based.
licence: US federal government works are generally not subject to copyright in the United States; specific portal terms NOT verified in this survey
licence_restrictions: Generally none for US government data, which is unusually favourable for republication. Confirm the portal's terms before publishing a derived dataset.
costs: Free. Cost is storage and compute for bulk analysis, plus entity-resolution effort. Estimate.
privacy: Public records about agencies and corporate recipients. Your queries are visible to the portal.
alternatives: SAM.gov for entity registration and contract-opportunity data
FPDS for the underlying federal procurement data feed
State and municipal procurement portals for local surveillance purchases, which are often where the interesting ones are
blockers: Classified and some national-security procurement excluded; recipient naming requires entity resolution before aggregation
summary: Official US federal spending portal with searchable and bulk-downloadable award data covering contracts, grants and subawards…
oss_detail: Hosted service or proprietary software — governed by service terms, not a software licence
